paper_title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by iterating a shared block of layers, but most evaluations compare at fixed model size, conflating architectural advantage with extra FLOPs. We study looping on Mixture-of-Experts Transformers while closely matching per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters, and KV cache. Through a series of ablations, we arrive at a recipe we call SMELT (Sparse MoE Transformer, middle layers Loop Twice), which loops the middle half of layers twice while matching the unlooped Baseline on all three budgets. We scale SMELT across four sizes up to 54B non-embedding parameters and fit a separate Chinchilla-style scaling law for each architecture. SMELT's loss drops faster with compute, saving 6.8--18.0\% of training FLOPs on the compute-optimal frontier. The advantage transfers to downstream benchmarks beyond what validation loss predicts, is largest on Code, and grows with sample length and the number of in-context examples. Mechanistic analysis shows that the second visit reduces the attention sink and redirects mass toward content-relevant tokens, an inductive bias that may underlie the observed performance gains. These results show that looping can improve Transformers even under budget matching, offering a practical recipe that turns depth reuse into measurable gains.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Looped Transformers increase models effective depth by repeating shared block of layers rather than stacking new ones [18]. The idea has drawn intense recent interest: looped models match or exceed unlooped models several times their size on arithmetic, multi-hop induction, and math [22, 54, 68], and learn algorithmic procedures in context at fraction of the parameter count [64]. Since effective depth sets how many sequential computation steps each token receives [40, 43], looping promises reasoning capability without additional parameters. But fraction of the parameter count is not fraction of the cost: looping 12-layer model to 24 executed layers stores half the weights, yet spends roughly 24-layer models per-token FLOPs and needs its full KV cache. Prior evaluations often keep the stored parameter count fixed while increasing recurrent depth [22, 47], or emphasize parameter efficiency relative to larger untied models [64, 68]; in either case the reported gains conflate architectural advantage with uncontrolled extra computation. Whether looping has an architectural advantage beyond this extra computation is unknown. Schwethelm et al. [55] control for this: they hold per-token FLOPs fixed for dense model and find that recurrences contribute like r0.46 unique-block equivalents, but fixing FLOPs also shrinks the looped models unique parameters, so the deficit may reflect parameter loss rather than flaw in looping itself. clean answer requires holding three budgets all fixed at once: 1) per-token FLOPs, which set training and inference cost; 2) total parameters, which bound knowledge (a) The SMELT recipe. (b) Compute-optimal frontier. (c) Downstream accuracy. Figure 1 SMELT overview and main results. (a) The SMELT recipe on compute-matched MoE Baseline: loop the middle 50% of layers twice, narrow the hidden dimension, raise the expert count to recover total parameters, and scale the looped residuals by 1/2, alongside smaller attention head size at higher GQA ratio that holds KV cache nearly unchanged across the extra layer executions. Together they closely match per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters, and KV cache (Section 3). (b) Compute-optimal loss under separate Chinchilla-style scaling fits at compute-equivalent sparsity 97% (defined in Section 3.1). SMELTs frontier drops faster; at = 1021 FLOPs it reaches the same loss with 14.7% less compute (Section 4). (c) Downstream accuracy at the 1.6B scale (54B non-embedding parameters, 97%), over the five DCLM Core categories (Appendix E), abbreviated on the axes as Reading (Comprehension), Knowledge (World Knowledge), Commonsense (Reasoning), Language (Understanding) and Symbolic (Problem Solving), with MMLU on its own axis. Each axis is the unweighted mean accuracy over its tasks. SMELT leads the Baseline on all six axes. capacity; and 3) KV cache, which limits servable context length. Mixture-of-Experts Transformers make this budget matching feasible: looped model can pay for its extra visit by narrowing the hidden dimension, and because MoE decouples total parameters from per-token FLOPs [20, 56], it can recover the lost capacity by raising expert count rather than giving it up. KV cache parity is restored separately by adjusting the head size and GQA ratio. Under this matching, we search the loop design space through three ablations and find three rules: 1) loop the middle half of layers rather than the full stack, 2) give the looped model larger effective depth-to-width ratio than the Baseline, and 3) loop twice rather than three or four times. Together these lock in recipe we call SMELT, Sparse MoE Transformer whose middle layers Loop Twice (Figure 1; Section 3). We scale the recipe up to 54B non-embedding parameters across four model sizes and four sparsity levels, comparing SMELT against the Baseline at each grid point. SMELT reaches lower loss than the Baseline at every scale and sparsity level. To predict how the advantage evolves at scale, we fit separate Chinchilla-style scaling laws [27] for the two architectures. SMELTs loss drops faster with both compute and data, and the CE Gain increases across the fitted compute range (Section 4). Beyond aggregate validation loss, we examine downstream benchmarks and per-domain performance. On DCLM [39] and MMLU [24], SMELT outperforms the Baseline in nearly all matched pairs, with an improvement that exceeds what the validation loss gap alone would predict. We also find that among training domains, Code benefits the most. The advantage is further amplified on longer samples and when more in-context demonstrations are available, suggesting that looping becomes more valuable as the input grows richer in retrievable structure (Section 5). To build intuition for the advantages observed above, we examine what the looped layers compute differently on their second visit. We find that the experts selected and the tokens attended to overlap substantially across the two visits, while the residual updates grow substantially larger and stay aligned, indicating that the second visit amplifies the first rather than overwriting it. Within the attention mechanism, values change more than queries and keys, and the attention sink is broadly reduced, redirecting mass toward content-relevant tokens, 2 which may relate to the observed ICL advantage (Section 6). Our results show that looping can improve Transformers even under budget matching, with particularly strong gains on structured data and in-context learning tasks. Together with the growing body of work exploring looped language models from complementary angles [22, 47, 54, 55, 68], they suggest that looping is robust and increasingly well-understood design axis.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Looped Transformers. The Universal Transformer [18] introduced weight sharing across depth, applying shared block iteratively to decouple effective depth from unique parameter count. Huginn [22] scales this idea to 3.5B parameters with preluderecurcoda layout (242 layers at its largest scale) that loops the middle 50%, establishing the template that most subsequent work adopts: an unshared entry block, shared middle block that is iterated, and an unshared exit block. Ouro [68] takes different partition: it loops the entire L-layer stack at 1.42.6B. Both show that looped models match or exceed much larger unlooped models on reasoning benchmarks. recurring finding across this body of work is that the middle layers benefit most from repetition. Saunshi et al. [54] compare looped models against both iso-parameter and iso-FLOP baselines: looped models have worse perplexity than the iso-FLOP baseline but disproportionately improve reasoning tasks, and iterating only middle span, the prelude-recur-coda layout above, further improves perplexity over full-stack looping. Kapl et al. [30] report that, among the block placements tested in their setting, adapting localized middle block for looping yields the strongest overall results. related but untied construction appears in SOLAR [32], whose depth-up-scaling method also targets the middle layers, duplicating them to grow pretrained model before continued pretraining. ALBERT [35] shares weights across all layers for parameter efficiency, an early instance of full cross-layer tying that predates the partial-loop designs above. Beyond the choice of which layers to loop, other work explores how to loop: Relaxed Recursive Transformers [4] add per-layer LoRA adapters to relax strict weight tying, and Mixture-of-Recursions [5] routes each token to learned recursion depth. Among these studies, Saunshi et al. additionally report an iso-FLOP comparison in which the looped model uses fewer unique parameters than the untied baseline [54]. RINS [3] matches total training compute by training its early-block recursive model on fewer tokens than its baseline, whereas we additionally match the token budget. Most other works above compare looped models against parameter-matched baselines, so the reported gains conflate architectural advantage with the extra FLOPs that repetition spends; whether looping helps or hurts under jointly matched compute and token budgets remains open. Mixture-of-Experts and loop recurrence. Answering the question above requires holding three budgets fixed at once: per-token FLOPs, total parameters, and KV cache  (Table 1)  . MoE makes this feasible by decoupling total parameters from per-token FLOPs [20, 56]: looped model can pay for its second visit by narrowing the hidden dimension, then recover the lost capacity by adding experts. MoEUT [15] proposes an MoE-based Universal Transformer that, for the first time, matches standard Transformers on language modeling. Lee et al. [36] find that sparse layers are critical to scaling looped models, because routing divergence across visits recovers expressivity lost to weight tying. Several concurrent works train MoE Looped Transformers at scale: LoopMoE [10] matches total parameters and per-token FLOPs at 3B and 9B; Gao et al. [21] train 6B and 20B models under wall-clock matching and independently find two loop steps optimal, corroborating our loop-count ablation (Section 3.5). Knupp et al. [33] (DREAMER) recurrently apply single MoE layer 1632 times with attention over previous depths under matched FLOPs, parameters, and memory; we view this single-layer recurrence as closer to implicit-depth models than to the block-level looping studied here. Chen et al. [11] share universal expert pool across layers, converting depth into virtual MoE width rather than looping the full layer block. These concurrent studies show that looping improves MoE models at individual scales. We ask complementary question: does the advantage hold across full scaling ladder when per-token FLOPs, total parameters, and KV cache are all matched? Matches wall-clock training time rather than per-token FLOPs. Scaling laws. Kaplan et al. [31] established power-law relations between loss, model size, and training tokens. Hoffmann et al. [27] (Chinchilla) refined the compute-optimal allocation and showed that parameters and tokens should scale at roughly equal rates with compute. For MoE models, Clark et al. [12] and Abnar et al. [1] extend these laws with routing variables such as expert count and sparsity; Li et al. [38] study the conditions under which MoE surpasses dense models at equal resources. Recent work extends these analyses to looped architectures. Schwethelm et al. [55] fit joint scaling law under an iso-depth protocol that holds effective depth (and therefore FLOPs and KV cache) fixed while reducing unique parameters. In their law, the effective parameter count of the recurrent block is Nonce + r0.46 Nrec: recurrent executions contribute like r0.46 unique-block equivalents. The sublinear exponent means recurrence yields diminishing capacity per iteration, so the looped model loses at matched compute. Prairie et al. [47] fit compute-optimal recurrence at fixed unique parameter count, but depth, inference FLOPs, and KV cache all grow with r, so the fit cannot separate the per-parameter sharing cost from the growing budgets. These two results bracket the question from opposite sides: Schwethelm et al. price loopings cost at fixed depth, Prairie et al. find loopings benefit at fixed parameters. We fit separate Chinchilla-style surface for each architecture on MoE models while closely matching per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters, and KV cache, which lets us isolate the architectural effect and measure the compute saving on the frontier (Section 4). Attention sinks. Autoregressive Transformers concentrate attention mass on initial tokens regardless of semantic content. Xiao et al. [63] identify this attention-sink phenomenon and exploit it for streaming inference; Gu et al. [23] characterize when sinks emerge during pretraining; Sun et al. [58] link them to massive activations in the residual stream, with an analogous register effect in vision models [16]; Barbero 4 et al. [6] argue that sinks counteract over-mixing and therefore strengthen as depth grows, trend also observed geometrically by Ruscio et al. [52]; and Qiu et al. [48] show that query-dependent sigmoid gate after attention strongly mitigates the sink in the evaluated models. These works treat the sink as static property of trained model. Our mechanistic analysis (Section 6) adds dynamic observation: within single forward pass, second weight-tied visit reduces sink mass and redirects it toward content-relevant tokens.

3.1 Training protocol
We write Baseline for the standard unlooped MoE Transformer and Looped Transformer for the variant that
repeats a contiguous span of m layers r times. The ablations in Sections 3.3–3.5 sweep both m and r; the
values they select define SMELT in Section 3.5. All runs share the same architecture template, optimizer,
data, and evaluation. Only the loop configuration (span, count, and effective depth) and the matched

this prevents correlated weight-tied updates from inflating the residual stream across visits.

We report matched Baseline / Looped Transformer pairs at 85%, 95%, and 97%; the same label applies to both architectures in all figures. Optimizer and schedule. We use AdamW [41] with warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedule [28]. The stable phase trains at constant learning rate over 196,075 steps with global batch size of 256 sequences (1M tokens per step). From each stable run we branch six cosine-decay schedules at steps 10,000, 20,000, 50,000, 100,000, 150,000, and 196,075, each decaying over 10B additional tokens. The six branch points give six token horizons per configuration. Data. We pretrain on an internal corpus. The stable phase of the WSD schedule consumes 205B tokens; each cosine-decay branch then trains on 10B additional tokens drawn from fresh data not seen during the stable phase, bringing the longest branch to approximately 215B tokens with no repeated data. All matched Baseline / SMELT pairs at the same scale and sparsity level are trained on identical token sequences. The held-out validation set covers 39 individual sources grouped into five categories: Code, Math/STEM, Knowledge, Finance, and Web. Training sequences are packed into 4096-token contexts with segment-level attention masks, where each segment is one document within the packed context. Evaluation. We score three metrics throughout. Validation loss is the token-weighted cross-entropy on the held-out validation set, averaged across all 39 sources. The other two come from the 22-task DCLM Core suite [39], evaluated with 10 random few-shot seeds per few-shot task and BOS-preserving truncation (details in Appendix E). The seven zero-shot tasks in the suite are deterministic and run once. DCLM Core is the mean centered accuracy over the 22 tasks (rescaled so that the DCLM-v2 reference baseline maps to zero). We define DCLM Completion as the token-weighted cross-entropy on the gold answer tokens of the nine tasks in the suite that ask for free-form answer rather than choice among options (lower is better). We also run MMLU 5-shot [24] and report it on its own, as it is widely used as standalone benchmark. To prevent benchmark contamination, we filtered known evaluation items from the pretraining corpus before training.

sections.title: 3.2 Matching as a compute-allocation problem
sections.content: We care about three quantities when we compare the Looped Transformer with the Baseline. Total parameters control how much knowledge model can memorize; per-token FLOPs set inference and training cost; KV cache determines the longest context deployment can serve. To attribute performance gaps primarily to architecture, we closely match all three between the Looped Transformer and the Baseline. Consider the cost of looping. standard MoE Transformer with physical layers spends per-token training FLOPs proportional to 2, where is the hidden dimension. When we loop contiguous span of layers times, the effective depth grows to Leff = + (r1) m, and FLOPs grow in proportion, while total parameters stay the same. To keep per-token FLOPs fixed, we must shrink the model elsewhere: we narrow or reduce L. That shrinkage also cuts total parameters and KV cache, so we must compensate on three axes at once. Table 2 lists the three budgets, the adjustment that holds each, and the residual mismatch after matching. Suppose we want Looped Transformer at 200M, 95% that loops the middle 6 of its 12 layers twice, executing 18 layers in total. The matched Baseline has = 12, hidden dimension = 1280, and 192 experts per layer (1.33 109 training FLOPs per token, 3.87 109 total non-embedding parameters). The 6 extra layer executions cost FLOPs, so we narrow from 1280 to 1056 to keep per-token FLOPs close. Narrowing also shrinks every experts FFN, which reduces total parameters. To recover them, we raise the per-layer expert count from 192 to 288. Expert count is uniform across all layers in both architectures. After both adjustments, per-token FLOPs land at 1.37 109 (+2.9% vs. the Baselines 1.33 109), total parameters at 3.89 109 (+0.4%), and KV cache within 4%. Both FLOPs counts are measured at the mean document length within the packed 4096-token contexts (since segment-level masks restrict attention to each document) and include the attention cost that scales with that length. sections.title: 4 Scaling Laws and Compute Savings
sections.content: The three ablations in Section 3 locked the SMELT recipe, but they all ran at the 200M scale (up to 3.9B non-embedding parameters). Does the advantage survive when models grow to tens of billions of parameters? This section scales the recipe across four sizes up to 54B non-embedding parameters, fits separate scaling surface for each architecture, and quantifies how much compute SMELT saves.

sections.title:
4.1 The SMELT recipe scales across the grid
We apply the budget matching protocol and the locked recipe from Sections 3.1–3.5 to the full 4 × 4 grid: four
scales (100M / 200M / 600M / 1.6B) crossed with an S=0% dense-reference control and three sparse levels
S ≈ {85%, 95%, 97%}. Each cell trains a matched Baseline / SMELT pair under the shared WSD schedule
from Section 3.1. The six cosine-decay branches per run (Section 3.1) yield six token horizons, which provide
the variation along the data axis needed to fit the data term of the scaling law (Section 4.2). Forking decay
branches from one stable run is cheaper than training a separate run per horizon, and annealed checkpoints
are the ones that reflect converged loss [28, 61]. That gives 32 runs, 16 × 6 = 96 matched Baseline / SMELT
pairs, and 192 evaluation endpoints.

sections.title:
4.2 Scaling form and compute efficiency gain
Scaling form. Kaplan et al. [31] established power-law relations between loss, model size, and training tokens.
The Chinchilla law [27] recasts the joint dependence as an additive form L(N, D) = E + AN −a + KD−c:

sections.content: Section 5.3 shows that SMELTs advantage grows with the number of in-context examples. To understand why, we study Dyck-language bracket matching, demonstration-sensitive exact-match task where the correct answer is unambiguous: to close bracket, the model must retrieve the matching opening symbol from demonstration in the prompt. This lets us trace, at the individual token level, whether the second visit improves retrieval of the right demonstration. Setup. We construct nested Dyck prompts at {1, 2, 4, 8} shots, with three fixed target positions whose correct closing symbol already appears in the 1 prefix. Each shot presents an input bracket sequence followed by its completion; we call the completion tokens that follow its Output: marker the demonstration answer. For each scale, we identify the Dyck head : we ablate each attention head in the repeated block one at time and select the head whose removal increases Dyck perplexity the most. We then visualize this heads full attention pattern to see where mass moves between the two visits. The attention sink nearly vanishes on the second visit. Figure 18 shows the Dyck heads attention map at 1.6B for = 4 example. On visit 1, the head concentrates mass on the attention sink at the segment-start BOS token and on nearby positions, as if the model does not yet know where to look. On visit 2, the sink nearly vanishes: mass shifts from BOS onto the demonstration answers in the prefix. The difference row makes the redistribution explicit. Averaged over the three targets, BOS mass falls from 0.60 to 0.02 while the demonstration answers rise from 0.24 to 0.85. We suspect this pattern is related to the ICL advantage reported in Section 5.3: more demonstrations give the second visit more answer spans to attend to, and the sink reduction frees mass to reach them. 21 Figure 18 Token-level attention map for the Dyck head at 1.6B, 85%, Dyck = 4. The Dyck head is the head in the repeated block whose ablation raises Dyck perplexity the most, identified separately at each scale. Rows are the three prediction targets; columns are key positions. Top: visit 1; middle: visit 2; bottom: difference. Orange marks are the 11 demonstration-answer tokens of the four shots, the completions that follow each shots Output: marker. Averaged over the three targets, the second visit cuts BOS mass from 0.60 to 0.02 and lifts demonstration-answer mass from 0.24 to 0.85, so the sink loses almost exactly what the demonstrations gain. The sink reduction generalizes beyond Dyck. Dyck is controlled task; does the same sink reduction occur on general pretraining data? We repeat the measurement on the full 1M-token held-out sample spanning all five source categories. The per-head heatmap (Figure 19a) shows that the bright, high-mass cells in visit 1 cool broadly on visit 2. We further find that this reduction goes against the ordinary depth trend. Figure 19b compares SMELT and the unlooped Baseline at the same physical depth: in the Baseline, sink mass grows toward later layers, consistent with the sink strengthening with depth in standard Transformers [6, 52], whereas SMELTs visit 2 lies below visit 1 throughout the repeated block. The second visit thus reverses the depth trend instead of inheriting the larger sink that its later position in the execution trace would predict; Appendix shows all four scales.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: We demonstrate that depth reuse is net win for MoE Transformers under budget matching. By searching the loop configuration space under budget matching, we identify the SMELT recipe, which loops the middle half of layers twice at larger effective depth-to-width ratio and consistently beats the Baseline across four scales and four sparsity levels, saving 6.818.0% of training compute on the frontier. The advantage extends beyond validation loss: on downstream benchmarks the gain exceeds what validation loss predicts, concentrates on structured data and long samples, and grows with in-context examples. Our mechanistic probes find consistent internal signature: the second visit reuses retrieval coordinates, amplifies residual writes, and frees attention mass from the sink. This suggests that looping acts as refinement step rather than simply adding capacity. Several directions remain open. Due to compute constraints, we conduct the design ablations at the 200M scale (up to 3.9B non-embedding parameters); the optimal loop span or count may differ at larger scales. We also study only the simplest form of looping: repeating contiguous block with fully shared weights. Richer variants relax this in different directions, including per-visit low-rank adapters [4], token-level adaptive recursion depth [5], learned halting [18, 19], block-selective sharing [30], and cross-token state reuse [9]. Whether these designs preserve or amplify the CE Gain under budget matching is left to future work. Separately, our budget matching equates arithmetic FLOPs, parameters, and KV-cache size, not wall-clock cost; serial 22 (a) Per-head segment-start attention mass at 1.6B. Visit 1 (left) concentrates mass on the segment start; visit 2 (right) reduces it across nearly every head. (b) Sink mass at matched physical depth. The bottom axis indexes Baseline physical layers; the top axis indexes SMELT execution layers. The Baseline grows with depth; SMELT visit 2 stays below visit 1. Figure 19 Segment-start attention mass (the attention sink) on the 1M-token held-out sample (S 85%). The second visit reduces the sink across nearly all heads and layers, running counter to the Baselines depth trend at matched physical depth. block re-execution and sparse routing might introduce hardware-efficiency gaps that require systems-level optimization to close. Finally, understanding exactly which mechanisms inside the second visit are responsible for the gain remains an open question; our probes in Section 6 offer descriptive starting point, and we expect future work to build on it toward causal account. Taken together, our results suggest that weight sharing across depth is viable axis for improving language models at matched compute, complementary to the established axes of scaling width, depth, and expert count. We look forward to seeing how far this axis can be pushed as compute budgets and model scales continue to grow.

sections.title: E Downstream Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: This appendix defines the downstream metrics, multi-seed protocol, and task categorization referenced by the main text. Task suite. We evaluate on the 22-task DCLM Core suite [39] and, separately, on MMLU 5-shot [24]. MMLU is not part of the official DCLM Core set but is widely used as standalone benchmark; we report it individually rather than folding it into our aggregate metrics. We use the v2 centered-accuracy baselines released by the DCLM project. Table 11 lists the full taskcategory mapping. DCLM Core (centered accuracy). For each task with raw accuracy at and DCLM-v2 reference baseline ρt (the Random baseline field in DCLMs evaluation metadata), the centered score is ct = at ρt 1 ρt , (11) so that 0 corresponds to the DCLM-v2 reference baseline and 1 to perfect accuracy. DCLM Core is the unweighted mean of ct over the 22 tasks. DCLM Completion (gold-completion micro loss). Nine of the 22 tasks ask for free-form answer rather than choice among options, so every item in them has gold answer string: CoQA, SQuAD, Jeopardy, 34 LAMBADA, BB QA Wikidata, BB CS Algorithms, BB Dyck Languages, BB Operators, and BB Repeat Copy. For each item we compute the per-token cross-entropy loss on the ground-truth answer tokens (the gold completion). DCLM Completion is the token-weighted (micro) average of these losses over all items of those nine tasks. Because it is loss rather than an accuracy, lower is better. This metric complements Core by providing continuous, fine-grained signal that is less affected by the discretization inherent in accuracy. Multi-seed protocol. Each few-shot task is evaluated with 10 independent random seeds that determine the selection and ordering of the few-shot demonstrations. Reported scores are the mean over these 10 runs. Zero-shot tasks (e.g. LAMBADA, Winograd) are deterministic and therefore evaluated with single run. All evaluations preserve the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token when truncating context to the models maximum sequence length.
